clue.text: Through which Miss Swancourt observed Mr Smith

definitions.text: Through which Miss Swancourt observed Mr Smith

parts.words: Through which Miss Swancourt observed Mr Smith
parts.note: Elfride Swancourt and Stephen Smith are the lovers in Thomas Hardy's early novel; the clue describes the organs she looked at him with, which give the book its title

explanation.surface: A question about what a Victorian heroine looked at her suitor through.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy's 1873 novel is named for Elfride Swancourt's eyes; the clue pretends to ask about a window or spyglass.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyes are what anyone sees through, and Hardy's title names the heroine's pair.

clue.text: Xanadu poet with German in a fit of anger

indicators.note: the German word for 'with' is placed inside the phrase for a fit of anger

parts.note: a fit of anger is a rage, so A RAGE
mit is the German word meaning with

explanation.surface: Coleridge's Xanadu poet storms about with a German companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Xanadu poet' points at Coleridge, but Simon Armitage wrote the poem-film Xanadu (1992).
explanation.definitionFit: Simon Armitage, later Poet Laureate, wrote the verse film Xanadu about a Rochdale housing estate.

clue.text: Liberated madman near capturing Heather in Dreiser reverie

indicators.note: the rearranged letters hold the plant name inside them
the letters of madman near are set free from their order and rearranged

parts.note: erica is the botanical name for heather

explanation.surface: A freed lunatic seizes a moorland plant during a daydream about a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberated' gives the anagram ANAMNDREAM, which 'capturing' wraps round the plant. The title is really Mailer's novel; Dreiser's An American Tragedy is the near-miss, but the phrase fits the dream his fiction chases.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreiser's novels chart the national fantasy of rising from poverty to wealth, the classic dream of the United States.

clue.text: "I'm the last of the -— mommas" (Jack Yellen)

definitions.text: "I'm the last of the -— mommas" (Jack Yellen)

parts.words: "I'm the last of the -— mommas" (Jack Yellen)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation: the missing hyphenated word completes the title of Jack Yellen's song made famous by Sophie Tucker

explanation.surface: A song lyric with a word left blank for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Yellen wrote 'Last of the Red Hot Mamas' (1928) for the vaudeville star Sophie Tucker.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank is filled by the adjective for passionate or fiery, completing Yellen's lyric.

clue.text: Stout snake

definitions.meaning: a work by Rex Stout, his first Nero Wolfe mystery (1934)
a venomous pit viper of tropical America

explanation.surface: A fat serpent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' looks like an adjective for the snake, but it is the American crime writer Rex Stout.
explanation.definitionFit: Rex Stout's debut detective novel bears the name of the venomous Central American pit viper.

clue.text: A great deal I got from French novelist

parts.note: a great deal is a lot

explanation.surface: Someone gets plenty out of reading a French writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre Loti was the pen name of the French naval officer who wrote exotic romances like Pêcheur d'Islande.

clue.text: Smith recorded his song, accompanied by trumpets?

definitions.text: Smith recorded his song, accompanied by trumpets?

parts.words: Smith recorded his song, accompanied by trumpets?
parts.note: the trumpets are the calls of a large tusked beast, the singer of a song set down by a writer named Smith

explanation.surface: A musician named Smith cut a record with a brass section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trumpets' suggests brass instruments; here it is the noise the animal makes.
explanation.definitionFit: The great pachyderm famously trumpets, so its song comes with that call built in.

clue.text: Characterised as pleasant play by its author (but it's impossible to be sure)

definitions.text: Characterised as pleasant play by its author
definitions.meaning: Shaw grouped this comedy among his Plays Pleasant
a stock phrase meaning nobody can predict the outcome

explanation.surface: A playwright calls his own comedy pleasant, though one can never be certain.
explanation.walkthrough: George Bernard Shaw published four comedies as Plays Pleasant (1898); this is one.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's comedy shares its title with the everyday idiom for uncertainty about what will happen.

clue.text: Slyest form of writers' manners

indicators.note: the word slyest is put into a new form, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: The most cunning kind of authorial behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: An author's style is the characteristic manner of the prose, so the plural covers several writers' ways of writing.

clue.text: River of the ancient world, possibly renamed

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of renamed may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: An ancient river may have been given a new name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maeander of Asia Minor was a winding river so famous for its loops that its name became a verb.

clue.text: Panel of Philpotts

parts.note: a play by Eden Phillpotts whose title is a group of twelve people sitting in judgment

explanation.surface: A committee belonging to someone called Philpotts.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve citizens hearing a trial form a panel, and Eden Phillpotts gave his drama that title.

clue.text: Mrs Behn's predator's further adventures by Conrad?

definitions.meaning: Aphra Behn's comedy about a roaming cavalier, which she followed with a Part II

explanation.surface: Aphra Behn's hunter has a sequel, possibly written by Conrad.
explanation.walkthrough: Aphra Behn's play of 1677 and Conrad's novel share the title; a rover is a wanderer or pirate, hence 'predator'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rover is a roaming pirate or wanderer, the title both of Behn's comedy and of Conrad's Napoleonic novel.

clue.text: Personification of the moon as satellite

definitions.meaning: a poetic name for the moon, from the Titaness linked with Artemis
one of the moons of Saturn

explanation.surface: The moon is shown in human form as a satellite.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek Titaness's name became a poetic title for the moon and was given to a moon of Saturn.

clue.text: "They hatch cockatrice' eggs, and weave the — —" (Isaiah)

definitions.text: "They hatch cockatrice' eggs, and weave the — —" (Isaiah)

parts.words: "They hatch cockatrice' eggs, and weave the — —" (Isaiah)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Isaiah 59:5 in the King James Bible, where the wicked spin something flimsy and deadly

explanation.surface: A Bible verse about the wicked with two words left blank.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaiah compares the plots of evildoers to the silk trap an arachnid spins.

clue.text: Hold maintained by Rudge

definitions.meaning: Barnaby Rudge in Dickens keeps a talking raven of this name

explanation.surface: Something is held on to by a man called Rudge.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens's Barnaby Rudge has a pet raven named Grip, so 'maintained' means kept as a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm clasp is a hold, and Barnaby Rudge keeps the raven of that name.

clue.text: One of the craftsmen given clear instructions by Salinger?

definitions.text: One of the craftsmen given clear instructions by Salinger?

parts.words: One of the craftsmen given clear instructions by Salinger?
parts.note: Salinger's title Raise High the Roof Beam

explanation.surface: A workman receives explicit orders from the author of Catcher in the Rye.
explanation.definitionFit: Salinger's novella title commands woodworkers to lift a roof beam, so each is one of those tradesmen.

clue.text: The Sandcastle?

parts.note: the ... tower at Sandycove, where Ulysses opens, read as a castle at Sandy(cove)

explanation.surface: A child's construction on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulysses begins in the Martello tower at Sandycove, Dublin; these round forts were built along coasts against Napoleon.
explanation.definitionFit: A coastal round fort is a small castle, and Joyce's stands at Sandycove.

clue.text: First friends of Locksley Hall

parts.note: Tennyson's Locksley Hall opens by addressing companions, so its first word is a term for friends

explanation.surface: The earliest friends made at a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's poem begins 'Comrades, leave me here a little'.
explanation.definitionFit: Companions in arms or in politics are friends, and the poem's first word hails them.

clue.text: Cowardly horse parade

definitions.meaning: belonging to Noël Coward, whose spectacular play of 1931 has this title

explanation.surface: A timid mount on parade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cowardly' looks like timid; it means by Noël Coward.
explanation.definitionFit: A procession of riders is the literal sense, and Coward borrowed it for his patriotic stage epic.

clue.text: Nymph in simple choice

indicators.note: in shows the nymph's name sits inside the words simple choice

explanation.surface: A nymph faces an easy decision.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the mountain nymph pined for Narcissus until only her voice was left.

clue.text: Italian poet's French count

definitions.meaning: belonging to the author of the Divine Comedy
Edmond, hero of Dumas's The Count of Monte Cristo

explanation.surface: A French nobleman belongs to an Italian poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Florentine poet's possessive matches the surname of Dumas's sailor turned Count of Monte Cristo.

clue.text: Splendid salesman returns in Verne's Nautilus?

indicators.note: in places the turned salesman inside the vessel

parts.note: Captain Nemo's Nautilus is a submarine, sub for short

indicators.note: returns means the word for a salesman goes back to front

parts.note: rep is short for a sales representative

explanation.surface: A salesperson comes back aboard Captain Nemo's craft and finds it wonderful.
explanation.definitionFit: Superb and splendid are synonyms for magnificent.

clue.text: Adelina Patti and a well-known kiss figure in his Reminiscences

definitions.text: Adelina Patti and a well-known kiss figure in his Reminiscences

parts.words: Adelina Patti and a well-known kiss figure in his Reminiscences
parts.note: the Italian conductor who composed the song Il Bacio (The Kiss) and wrote memoirs mentioning the soprano Patti

explanation.surface: A memoir recalls the opera singer and a famous kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: Luigi Arditi composed 'Il Bacio' and wrote My Reminiscences (1896); Patti sang his song.
explanation.definitionFit: Luigi Arditi was the conductor-composer whose waltz-song means the kiss and whose memoirs feature Patti.

clue.text: Odin was Lord of this Ring

definitions.text: Odin was Lord of this Ring

parts.words: Odin was Lord of this Ring
parts.note: the god's self-multiplying gold arm-ring in Norse myth, playing on Tolkien's Lord of the Rings

explanation.surface: The chief Norse god owned a ring, echoing Tolkien.
explanation.walkthrough: In Norse myth Odin's gold ring dripped eight new rings every ninth night.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse arm-ring forged by dwarfs belonged to the chief god, who placed it on Baldr's pyre.

clue.text: Subtle assistant

parts.note: in Jonson's The Alchemist the con man Subtle works with a housekeeper who goes by this name

explanation.surface: A discreet helper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subtle' reads as an adjective; it is Ben Jonson's fake alchemist, whose accomplice is called Face.
explanation.definitionFit: In Jonson's comedy the butler Jeremy, alias Face, is the confederate of Subtle.

clue.text: Donne's jumper

parts.note: a poem by John Donne about a tiny leaping insect that has bitten both lovers

explanation.surface: A sweater belonging to the poet John Donne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' is British for a sweater, but here it is a leaping insect, subject of Donne's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The little bloodsucking insect that jumps is the subject of Donne's seduction poem.

clue.text: Beryl Bainbridge's break with French painter

definitions.text: Beryl Bainbridge's break with French painter

parts.words: Beryl Bainbridge's break with French painter
parts.note: Bainbridge's novel A ... with Claud, the name of the French painter Claude Lorrain

explanation.surface: A novelist takes a holiday in the company of a French artist.
explanation.walkthrough: Beryl Bainbridge's 1967 novel is A Weekend with Claud; Claude Lorrain was a French landscape painter.
explanation.definitionFit: A short break from Saturday to Sunday, the time span in Bainbridge's title.

clue.text: Called by pretty girls, reportedly by Betjeman

parts.note: called means summoned
taken as written

indicators.note: reportedly means the word for pretty girls is heard rather than seen

parts.note: belles are beautiful women

explanation.surface: Someone was called on by attractive women, according to Betjeman.
explanation.definitionFit: Betjeman's 1960 verse autobiography takes its title from the church peals of his childhood.
